articles.title: A ‘yellow brick road’ was discovered 1,029 metres beneath the Pacific Ocean; scientists explain how volcanic rock and iron-rich deposits created the striking formation
articles.summary: A strange formation resembling a yellow brick road was discovered on the Pacific Ocean floor during an expedition by the Ocean Exploration Trust’s
articles.body: A strange formation resembling a yellow brick road was discovered on the Pacific Ocean floor during an expedition by the Ocean Exploration Trust’s research vessel E/V Nautilus. The structure was found at a depth of 1,029 metres near Nootka Seamount, within the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument. Its unusually regular pattern made it resemble a brick sidewalk, but scientists identified it as a natural geological formation.According to a report published by The Oceanography Society on the Ocean Exploration Trust’s 2022 field season, the formation likely consists of fractured hyaloclastite, a type of volcanic rock created when hot magma meets cold water. Researchers suggested that its yellow colour likely resulted from low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of the volcanic glass.Scientists spotted a yellow brick road 1,029 metres beneath the PacificThe unusual pattern was observed during an E/V Nautilus expedition in the Pacific. The formation lay at a depth of 1,029 metres near Nootka Seamount, inside Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument. Its fractures intersect at right angles, giving it the look of a brick sidewalk. The resemblance prompted the description ‘yellow brick road’, but the appearance did not indicate that people had built or laid anything there.The report identifies the feature as a geological formation on the seafloor. It was one of several discoveries documented during the vessel’s 2022 field season, when the team explored deep-ocean environments and used remotely operated and autonomous systems to investigate remote and poorly surveyed areas.Right-angled cracks gave the formation its unusual appearanceThe report explains that the formation likely consists of hyaloclastite. This rock forms when hot magma comes into contact with cold water, causing volcanic material to break into fragments. Scientists said the surface likely represents fractured hyaloclastite, rather than a constructed pathway.The cracks intersect at right angles, producing the unusually neat pattern that gives the site its road-like appearance. The geometry may look carefully arranged, but it is part of the rock’s natural structure. The report attributes the formation to volcanic activity on the seafloor. The report says the formation is natural, not human-made.How did volcanic glass develop its yellowish appearanceThe yellow appearance also has a natural explanation. According to the report, the colour likely developed through low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of the volcanic glass. This process changes the material after it forms, leaving iron oxyhydroxide that gives the surface its yellowish colour. Hydrothermal alteration refers to changes caused when heated fluids interact with rock. In this case, the report presents it as the likely reason for the colour. Together, the fractured rock, right-angled cracks and altered volcanic glass give the seafloor feature the appearance of a road, although it was formed through natural geological activity in the area.The 2022 field season documented several other deep-sea discoveriesThe yellow brick road was one finding from the 2022 field season aboard E/V Nautilus. The report describes a wider programme of seafloor mapping, remotely operated vehicle dives and work with autonomous systems. It records 120 uncrewed vehicle deployments during the season. The expeditions also documented deep-sea coral and sponge communities, fossilised whale bones and a fossilised Megalodon tooth.Researchers observed and collected a sea pen from the genus Solumbellula, marking its first recorded observation and collection in the Pacific, according to the report. The work combined exploration with scientific research and public outreach, allowing people on shore to follow discoveries through live broadcasts and ship-to-shore connections during the same field season.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Madagascar's giant flying foxes have become smaller over four decades; researchers found their skulls are around 6% smaller than those collected before the 1980s, raising concerns about hunting pressure
articles.summary: One of Madagascar’s largest bat species is showing a striking physical change, with researchers finding that its skulls have become approximately 6 per
articles.body: One of Madagascar’s largest bat species is showing a striking physical change, with researchers finding that its skulls have become approximately 6 per cent smaller over the past four decades. The findings, published in the Journal of Mammalogy on October 29, 2026, point towards a possible connection between shrinking body size and increased hunting pressure. The research, also reported by Science News and conservation-focused publications, raises fresh questions about how human activity is changing wildlife populations and threatening species already facing population decline. The Malagasy flying fox (Pteropus rufus), known for its impressive wingspan and fox-like facial features, is among the world's largest bats. Found across Madagascar, these fruit-eating mammals play an important ecological role by dispersing seeds and helping maintain forest ecosystems. The research was led by Emily Cornelius Ruhs and Steven Goodman of Chicago's Field Museum. To investigate the apparent change, the scientists examined 121 preserved specimens held in nine natural history museums across the United States and Europe. The specimens represented more than 150 years of the species' history. The team recorded measurements of 12 different features of the bats' skulls and teeth. Their analysis revealed that specimens collected before the 1980s had skulls that were, on average, 3.6 millimetres longer than those collected in subsequent decades. This represents a difference of approximately 6 per cent.Why hunting could be changing their sizeResearchers believe the timing of the physical change may be significant. Until the 1980s, flying foxes were largely hunted on a small scale to provide food for individual families and local communities. However, hunting gradually became more commercialised, with bats increasingly being sold in markets and served in restaurants.The researchers suspect that larger bats may have become easier targets because of their size and the greater amount of meat they provide. This could have resulted in disproportionate hunting of larger individuals, gradually changing the physical characteristics seen in subsequent generations. A report by Mongabay also highlighted the importance of the species as a food source in Madagascar, where flying foxes are hunted for both household consumption and commercial sale. Some hunters use nets, while others shoot the animals before selling them.However, hunting is not necessarily the only explanation. The researchers have also identified deforestation, changing climatic conditions and shifts in fruit availability as possible contributors. The study establishes a strong association between the increase in commercial hunting and the decline in skull size, but does not conclusively establish that hunting alone caused the change.A shrinking species faces wider conservation concernsThe findings are particularly concerning because Malagasy flying foxes are already facing pressure from multiple directions. Beyond their role as a food source, the bats are important seed dispersers and pollinators. By feeding on fruits and nectar and moving between trees, they help support forest regeneration and maintain Madagascar's biodiversity. Their slow reproductive rate makes the situation more complicated. The loss of larger, sexually mature individuals could potentially affect the population's ability to reproduce and recover from continued hunting pressure.A study of this kind also highlights why museum collections are valuable to conservation science. Preserved specimens offer researchers a rare opportunity to compare wildlife across generations and identify physical changes that might otherwise go unnoticed. The researchers believe further monitoring and stronger protection, particularly around breeding sites, will be important to safeguard the species. They also want to understand whether similar physical changes are occurring in other fruit bats hunted across Madagascar. The findings offer a reminder that human activity can leave lasting effects on wildlife, sometimes in ways that become visible only after decades of change.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Scientists scooped 11 endangered alpine spiny crayfish from a Victorian creek after bushfires in January, keeping the feisty creatures apart in a hatchery; months later, they are being returned to their home waters
articles.summary: Bushfires can threaten to wipe out an entire wildlife species, let alone one that is already endangered.
articles.body: Bushfires can threaten to wipe out an entire wildlife species, let alone one that is already endangered. This is a concern that has prompted many conservationists and scientists to take part in rescue operations. In Victoria, Australia, a group of scientists rushed to the rescue of the endangered alpine spiny crayfish during the January 2026 bushfires, rescuing a total of 11 from a creek. Months later, after being cared for in captivity, the creatures are finally making their way back to the waters they call home.According to an ABC News report dated November 7, 2026, scientists from the Arthur Rylah Institute rescued 11 of these crayfish from a creek near Lucyvale in the immediate aftermath of the fires. The concern was that the creatures could suffocate as debris and sediment entered the waterway, affecting the conditions they depended on to survive. Will Sowersby, a senior scientist at the Arthur Rylah Institute, explained to ABC News that without intervention, the species could disappear from some of these freshwater areas. The rescue was therefore not simply about moving a handful of creatures away from an immediate threat, but also about protecting a vulnerable population whose limited distribution makes it particularly susceptible to environmental disturbances.The feisty residents of a conservation hatcheryOnce rescued, the 11 crayfish were transported to the Snobs Creek conservation hatchery near Eildon, which is operated by the Victorian Fisheries Authority. They remained there while scientists waited for the water quality in their natural habitat to improve sufficiently for their return.However, keeping them alive in captivity presented an entirely different set of challenges. This was the first time alpine spiny crayfish had been taken into captivity, meaning hatchery staff were learning about their behaviour and care requirements as they went along. One of the more unexpected difficulties was just how aggressive the creatures could be towards one another. Dylan White, a senior conservation hatchery officer at Snobs Creek, told ABC News that the crayfish had to be housed separately because they would attack each other if kept together.It meant that the hatchery team had to make individual arrangements for the rescued animals, keeping them apart throughout their stay. While the creatures were no longer facing the immediate threat of deteriorating water conditions in the creek, their temporary home still required careful attention to ensure they remained healthy until they could be returned.Preparing for a future beyond the rescueThe return of the crayfish comes as the Victorian High Country gradually recovers from the Walwa-River Road bushfire, which burned approximately 121,000 hectares. Although the immediate danger has passed for the rescued animals, scientists are continuing to monitor the waterways and the surrounding habitat to understand how the species will fare in the months ahead.There is also a larger conservation question emerging from the experience. Scientists hope that alpine spiny crayfish could eventually become part of a captive breeding programme at the Snobs Creek hatchery. The hatchery itself has become an important centre for the rescue and care of vulnerable freshwater species following natural disasters. Its staff have also looked after other animals affected by Victoria's summer bushfires, including Macquarie perch and trout cod rescued from Seven Creek following the Longwood bushfire. More than 100 of these fish have already been released back into the wild. However, the work at the hatchery is not without its challenges for the staff, as each rescue brings a different set of requirements and, sometimes, the need to learn how to care for a species that has never been kept in captivity before.For the alpine spiny crayfish, the journey from a fire-affected creek to a conservation hatchery and eventually back to their home waters has been an atypical one. Their rescue also offers a reminder that the consequences of a bushfire are not always immediately visible. Beneath the surface of a stream, entire populations of small and often overlooked creatures can be at risk, making the work of protecting them just as important as restoring the landscapes we see above ground. With the country at risk of facing more natural disasters as climate change progresses, protection and rescue operations for species, particularly those already at a high risk of extinction, have become a need of the hour.Your child uses AI every day.
